target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is uniquely hands-on and educationally valuable
objection: Modern alternatives such as synthetic models, preserved specimens where appropriate, and computer simulations can teach anatomy and physiology equally well or better, so dissection is not necessary for the learning goals AG1 describes.

target: AG1’s assumption that dissection specimens are mostly harmless food-industry byproducts
objection: The animals used for dissections are typically obtained in inhumane ways, with roughly 99% caught in the wild; wild-capture reduces local populations and biodiversity, creating environmental harm that undercuts the educational justification.

target: AG1’s appeal to dissection as a standard educational practice
objection: Animal dissection is not required by AP Biology or Next Generation Science Standards, and medical education in the U.S. and Canada does not use animals for physician training, so the practice is unnecessary for meeting legitimate educational objectives.

target: AG1’s claim that opt-out or alternative assignments solve the ethical problem
objection: Requiring dissection still coerces students to handle dead animals or lose instructional time and full access to the curriculum, so opt-out does not eliminate the ethical exclusion and pressure placed on dissenting students.

target: AG1’s suggestion that byproduct sourcing makes dissection ethically acceptable
objection: Even if some specimens are byproducts, dissection still depends on killing animals for classroom use and cannot be justified as a reliable ‘no harm’ practice when effective alternatives exist.

target: AG1’s claim that schools can avoid ethical problems by allowing dissection only as an option
objection: Keeping dissection as an option still leaves the underlying harm in place because schools continue purchasing and preparing animals, so the practice should not remain a default classroom method when alternatives can meet the same goals.

target: AG1’s claim that fetal pigs and similar specimens are already dead byproducts and therefore do not create harm
objection: Even if some specimens are byproducts, dissection can still incentivize acquisition and preparation of animal remains through supply chains that depend on animals being caught or killed somewhere, so ‘byproduct-only’ sourcing does not justify the practice.

target: AG1’s argument that dissection is justified because it reuses animal bodies that would otherwise be discarded
objection: Using animal bodies as educational material still creates extra demand for those tissues and can incentivize breeding, raising, catching, and processing more animals upstream; it is not simply harmless waste reduction.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection uniquely provides tactile realism and real biological variability
objection: The ethical issue is not just whether dissection is educationally interesting; if comparable learning can be achieved with non-animal methods, then using dead sentient animals remains unnecessary exploitation and should be avoided.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection teaches valuable lab procedure and hands-on scientific skills
objection: The same procedural and safety skills can be taught with non-animal activities such as microscope labs, synthetic models, plant or yeast labs, pipetting and measurement exercises, and observational protocols, so carcass dissection is not required to develop lab competence.

target: AG1’s claim that high-quality alternatives are too costly or hard to implement in many schools
objection: Budget and implementation constraints do not justify using animals when dissection is not required by standards; the ethical response is to fund and design non-animal labs rather than keep carcass-based dissection as the default.
